items.prompt: What's the key difference between what git reset and git revert actually do to history?
choices: They're functionally identical; revert is just an older name for reset
reset moves the branch pointer backward (rewriting what the branch points to); revert adds a NEW commit that cancels out an old one, leaving history untouched and append-only
reset only works on files, revert only works on entire commits
revert deletes commits from the repository entirely; reset only hides them
items.explanation: This is the central distinction: reset rewrites what history a branch points to; revert never removes or rewrites anything — it adds a new commit whose effect is the inverse of an old one, keeping history append-only.

items.prompt: Which git reset mode can permanently delete uncommitted changes in your working directory, with no recovery path?
choices: --soft
--mixed (the default)
--hard
None of them touch the working directory
items.explanation: --soft only moves the branch pointer; --mixed additionally unstages but leaves working-directory file contents alone; --hard additionally overwrites the working directory to match the target commit, discarding any uncommitted changes with no undo.

items.prompt: Per L2's decision table, what's the single question that determines whether reset or revert is the safe choice for undoing a commit?
choices: How many lines of code the commit changed
Whether the commit has possibly already been pushed/shared with anyone else — reset is fine for purely local commits, revert is the default once sharing is possible
Whether the commit message follows conventional commit format
Whether the commit was made more than a day ago
items.explanation: The whole safety argument hinges on whether anyone else might already have a copy of the history being changed — reset rewriting purely local history costs nothing since nobody else has it; reset rewriting shared history creates real divergence for anyone who already pulled it.

items.prompt: In L3's first example, `git checkout HEAD -- config.json` is run while `feature.js` also has uncommitted changes. What happens to feature.js?
choices: It gets reset to its last-committed state too, since checkout affects the whole working directory
Nothing — checkout with a specific file path only restores that one file, leaving other uncommitted changes untouched
The command fails because feature.js also has uncommitted changes
feature.js gets staged automatically
items.explanation: checkout -- <file> (or the modern git restore <file>) is scoped to exactly the file(s) named — this is the narrow, safe use of checkout, distinct from checking out an entire branch or commit which would affect everything.

items.prompt: In L3's second example, `git reset --hard HEAD` deletes a newly-created, staged-but-never-committed file. Can this specific file be recovered afterward, e.g. via the reflog?
choices: Yes, the reflog can always recover any file lost to any git command
No — the reflog only helps recover commits that existed at some point; a file that was never committed at all was never captured by the reflog either, so there's no git-level recovery path
Yes, but only within 24 hours of the reset
No, but a fresh git init will regenerate the file
items.explanation: The reflog tracks where branch/HEAD pointers have been, which lets you recover commits that got orphaned by a reset — it has no record of working-directory content that was never actually committed, which is exactly why reset --hard on uncommitted-but-staged new files is genuinely unrecoverable.

items.prompt: Implement `chooseUndoStrategy({ isPushed, teamCoordinatedRewrite })` from L3: if the commit isn't pushed, return "reset". If it is pushed and there's no team-coordinated rewrite agreement, return "revert". If it's pushed AND there's a coordinated rewrite agreement, return "reset-with-force-push".

tests.description: not pushed, coordination flag irrelevant -> still reset

items.explanation: This directly encodes L2's decision rule: whether a commit is pushed determines whether rewriting it is safe by default; a coordinated rewrite is the one explicit, agreed exception even for pushed commits — everything else pushed falls back to revert, the append-only, always-safe default.
